chunks: (10) Muhammad ibn Hammam narrated that Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abdullah al-Khalanji narrated that Abu Hashim Dawud ibn al-Qassim al-Ja'fari said: 'We were with Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali al-Rida (peace be upon him) when the mention of al-Sufyani came up, and what has come in the narrations that his matter is inevitable. I said to Abu Ja'far: 'Does Allah change His determination concerning the inevitable?' He said: 'Yes.' We said to him: 'We fear that He may change His determination concerning the Qa'im.' He said: 'Indeed, the Qa'im is from the Promise, and Allah does not fail to perform the Promise.'

key_terms.السُّفْيَانِيُّ: Al-Sufyani, a key eschatological figure in Shia tradition
key_terms.الْقَائِمِ: The Qa'im, referring to Imam al-Mahdi
key_terms.الْمُحْتَوَمِ: The inevitable or firmly decided matter
key_terms.الْمِيعَادِ: The Promise, referring to Allah's guaranteed covenant regarding the Imam's appearance

ai.seo_question: Does Allah change His decree regarding the inevitable rise of the Mahdi?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Rida, the distinction is drawn between general divine decrees that may be altered by supplication or wisdom and the specific eschatological promise of the Mahdi's appearance, which is fixed and unchangeable. This highlights the Shia theological principle that while 'al-muhtam' (the inevitable) is often subject to divine discretion, the coming of the Qa'im is a definitive covenant (al-Mi'ad) that Allah will not break, providing certainty to the believers amidst the uncertainty of other signs like the Sufyani.
